x: Rusty Minecraft: a map for agents Minecraft: Java Edition 26.3 rewritten in Rust (wgpu): a fork of Horizon (MIT) that keeps its code, crate names ( horizon-* ), file names and environment variables ( HORIZON_* ). Vanilla is the specification wherever it has the feature. Read CONTRIBUTING.md once; this page tells you where things are. Feature → files → harness for the most-changed areas: docs/architecture.md . Rules that bite Never commit Mojang's files : game jars, assets, decompiled source, prepared resources ( .local/ ). tools/check_public_tree.py rejects them; git config core.hooksPath .githooks runs it on commit. Keep your runs away from real player data. Any game or launcher you start gets fresh mktemp -d folders in HORIZON_HOME (the game's data), HORIZON_LAUNCHER_HOME , XDG_DATA_HOME and XDG_CONFIG_HOME , plus HORIZON_LAUNCHER_NO_SELF_UPDATE=1 and HORIZON_NO_AUDIO=1 , and, for the launcher, HORIZON_LAUNCHER_TRASH , HORIZON_LAUNCHER_CLIPBOARD and HORIZON_LAUNCHER_DESKTOP pointing into the scratch home. Never write to ~/.local/share/{applications,horizon,horizon-launcher} or ~/.local/bin . Mark what an agent posts. A PR body starts with a line naming the person whose agent opened it and the tool: > 🤖 Opened by <login>'s AI agent (<tool, model>), not by <login> personally. , where <login> is the GitHub account the PR is opened from ( gh api user --jq .login ). Issues say "Filed by", reviews "Review by". Every comment starts with 🤖 Agent: . Write only as the person you work for: the lines on this page that name Ludovic are for his own agents (account ludovic111 ), never for anyone else's. Attribution. Commits end with a Co-Authored-By: line for the agent that wrote them, and PR bodies with that agent's own "Generated with" line. Example, Ludovic's agents (Claude Code on ludovic111 ): first line > 🤖 Opened by Ludovic's AI agent (Claude), not by Ludovic himself. , commits Co-Authored-By: Claude <model> <noreply@anthropic.com> , last line 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) . Everything players run is Rust, with one exception: the optional Java layer for Java mods ( crates/horizon-java , docs/java-mod-runtime.md ) embeds a JVM through JNI. It is behind the java-mods cargo feature, off by default (Settings > Java mods > Run their code), and runs on a Java the player already has, never a bundled one. Otherwise Python/Java only for dev tools and harness drivers in tools/ . Rusty Minecraft-only features follow docs/design-system.md and are off by default where they would change the vanilla look. Small PRs (< ~500 lines). Labels: feature (players get something new), skip-release (they see no change), none for a fix. Agents never add release-now : the maintainer decides it. Merges ship in batches of 5, or after 6 hours ( docs/release-flow.md ). Contributors first: gh pr list --state open --search <area> before you start; never duplicate theirs. x: Contributing to Rusty Minecraft Thanks for helping. Rusty Minecraft is Minecraft: Java Edition 26.3 rewritten in Rust, and the one rule that shapes everything is that it plays exactly like vanilla . This page is the short version of how we work; questions are welcome on Discord . This repository holds the game and the launcher, plus the tools, tests and docs that build, check and release them. The website (playhorizon.dev) is built in a separate repository from this one's README, docs/api/ and roadmap. Anything else (videos, Discord and other community material) lives elsewhere. Where to start: playhorizon.dev/hub . It shows what is being done now and next ( ROADMAP.md in the repository), the work board, good first tasks, and the forms to report a bug or suggest something. A pull request for a roadmap item carries its roadmap:<id> label; ideas go to the suggestion queue (the hub, or /suggest on Discord) rather than to issues, which are for bugs. Build it You need Rust (stable), Python 3.10+, JDK 25, and on Linux the ALSA and udev headers ( libasound2-dev libudev-dev ). Rusty Minecraft never downloads the game: it prepares its resources from your own copy of Minecraft 26.3, as described in Build from source . cargo run --release -p horizon-prepare -- --prepare --server-jar ~/Downloads/server.jar cargo run --release -p horizon-client The launcher is its own Cargo workspace in launcher/ ( cd launcher && cargo run ; on NixOS, nix-shell first). Vanilla first Wherever vanilla has a feature, vanilla is the specification, down to the order of random calls. "Parity" here means Rusty Minecraft gives the same results as the pinned 26.3 client and server for the same inputs, checked by a harness : a tools/test_*_parity.py script that runs a small Java oracle against the real game and a Rust probe against Rusty Minecraft, and compares their outputs. There are about 290 of them. Read the vanilla code before writing Rusty Minecraft's. tools/rea_vanilla.py queries the pinned game bytecode: python3 tools/rea_vanilla.py method net.minecraft.world.level.block.DispenserBlock dispenseFrom . Say in your pull request which vanilla classes and methods you followed. Gameplay changes come with a harness , new or extended, so the next change can't silently break them. The parity workflow shows how harnesses run; copy a nearby one. Rusty Minecraft's own features (the launcher, the new menus) follow the design system and are off by default wherever they would change the vanilla look. Everything players run is Rust. Python and Java are fine for dev tools and harness drivers in tools/ , never for player-facing code. The one exception is the optional Java layer for Java mods ( java-mod-runtime.md ): a JVM embedded through JNI, behind the java-mods cargo feature, off by default (a switch in Settings), on a Java the player already has. Nothing is bundled, and the game's own code stays Rust. Never commit game files, decompiled source or prepared resources ( .local/ ): tools/check_

Rusty Minecraft is a fork of Horizon , the Rust rewrite of Minecraft: Java Edition by Ludovic Marie and the Horizon contributors, released under the MIT licence (see LICENSE ). Nearly all of the game, the launcher and the tools here are their work. This fork continues it as its own version and adds a Java mod translation layer : a Fabric, Quilt, NeoForge or Forge mod jar put in the game folder becomes a content mod when the game starts, managed from the launcher's Settings > Java mods ( docs/java-mod-translation.md ). Horizon's GitHub workflows are parked in .github/upstream-workflows . Not an official Minecraft product. Not approved by or associated with Mojang or Microsoft. Rusty Minecraft contains no Minecraft code, assets or data: you need your own legally obtained copy of Minecraft: Java Edition 26.3. Download Rusty Minecraft has no releases of its own yet: build the launcher from source ( launcher/README.md ) and the game as below ( Build from source ). The launcher installs game builds from Horizon's releases until this fork publishes its own, so the game it installs is Horizon's, without this fork's changes; a game built from this repository has them. You need a Microsoft account that owns Minecraft: Java Edition (the launcher signs in with it, as other launchers do; see Microsoft account ) and a GPU with Vulkan or OpenGL 3.3 on Linux, Vulkan or DirectX 12 on Windows, or any Apple Silicon Mac. x: Horizon's server against vanilla 26.3: mixed bots, equal work (2026-10-18) This reruns ../server-mixed-2026-10-18/ with the bots' load made the same on both servers. In that run the explore bots flew as fast as each server sent them chunks. Horizon kept up and vanilla didn't, so Horizon sent 2.9 to 5.9 times as many chunks a second, and vanilla's walking bots got a fifth of the chunks Horizon's got. The comparison of tick times wasn't fair. Summary The work was equal at 1 and 10 bots. At 25 bots it was equal in chunks sent a second (158.6 against 157.6); vanilla was still catching up on chunks its bots hadn't had yet, see "Equal work" below. Every bot joined, none was dropped, no chunk was sent twice, and no bot ever waited for the chunk it stood in. Tick time (MSPT), same work: 1 bot: 1.8 ms on Horizon against 11.3 on vanilla; 10 bots: 4.7 against 34.3 ms; 25 bots: 11.7 against 50.5 ms. Vanilla dropped just under 20 TPS (19.8) and its worst 5-second P99 was 1388 ms, against Horizon's 130; 50 bots: Horizon ran at 23.8 ms (20 TPS). Vanilla's watchdog stopped its server 30 s after the last bot joined ("A single server tick took 60.01 seconds"). Memory: Horizon's RSS was 4.1 to 4.9 times smaller: 0.69 against 3.40 GB with one bot, 0.95 against 3.87 GB with 25, and 1.03 GB with 50. This replaces the first run in docs/server.md section 9, where the work wasn't equal. What was made equal The first run (PR #556) had three differences that made the comparison unfair. Each is fixed in the code that ran here: Refused moves. Vanilla pulls a player back when a move is too fast ("moved too quickly") or ends inside a block ("moved wrongly"). Horizon now runs both checks the way vanilla does (PR #586), so a bot that flies too fast is pulled back on both servers. Chunk sending. Vanilla paces chunks by the client's acknowledgements (PlayerChunkSender: one unacknowledged batch at first, then ten, each at most the client's desired chunks per tick). Horizon used to send twice as many per batch; it now paces them the same way (PR #586), and the bots acknowledge batches and ask for a rate the way vanilla's client does, so both servers send at the pace the client asks for. Chunks sent again while the bot still held them ( resent ) are counted: 0 on both servers in every run. Movement gated on chunks. A bot doesn't move while the chunk it stands in hasn't arrived (vanilla's client waits the same way), so a slower server isn't asked to teleport bots into terrain it hasn't sent. One difference isn't in Horizon yet: vanilla 26.3's locator bar (waypoints), which costs vanilla O(players²) work per move. Every vanilla run here sets gamerule locator_bar false , so neither server does it. Method tools/server_bench.py runs each configuration on a fresh server: the same server.properties on both (seed 12345, view and simulation distance 10, offline, creative, difficulty easy, sync-chunk-writes=true ), and gamerule respawn_radius 0 ; the server waits for Done , the bots join one a second, a 60-second warm-up, then 300 seconds of measurement; MSPT (average, P50, P95, P99) comes from each server's own /tick query , asked every 5 seconds on the console, so both measure themselves the same way (vanilla's ServerTickRateManager numbers, which Horizon reproduces); TPS is 20 while the average fits in 50 ms, else 1000 / MSPT; RSS and CPU are the server's whole process tree, once a second (100 % is one core); chunk counts come from the bots: chunks received per second, chunks no bot had before (new terrain), and pull-backs (position packets that move a bot back). The bots are horizon-bots (creative, flying 24 blocks above spawn, 20 moves a second): walk : flies to random points within 48 blocks of spawn at sprint speed (5.6 blocks a second); explore : flies straight outwards, by default at about 22 blocks a second, as fast as the server sends chunks. The Java layer's own classes Compiled by build.rs (feature jvm , with the JDK's javac --release 21 ) and defined in the JVM's system class loader before any mod loads ( src/jvm/mod.rs , superclasses first). All of it is written for Rusty Minecraft, from public documentation only: the class, method and field names and signatures are the public APIs mods compile against (vanilla 26.x's names, Fabric's, Mixin's), so a mod's bytecode links to them; no line comes from Mojang's, Fabric's or Mixin's code. net/minecraft/ : the Java API layer, a small part of vanilla's API with its names (docs/java-mod-runtime.md lists it). Values ( Identifier , BlockPos , Vec3 , Direction , Component ) are plain Java; game objects ( MinecraftServer , Level , ServerLevel , Entity , LivingEntity , Player , ServerPlayer , Block , BlockState , Item , ItemStack ) hold the game's handle (a level, an entity id, a block state id) and ask the game through dev/rustyminecraft/java/Host.java 's native methods. BuiltInRegistries.BLOCK and ITEM take a mod's registrations and hand them to the game. net/fabricmc/ : Fabric's facade: ModInitializer and the other entry points, FabricLoader , Event and EventFactory , and ServerTickEvents and ServerLifecycleEvents , which the game's hook points fire ( src/fabric.rs says which). org/spongepowered/asm/mixin/injection/callback/ : what a mixin handler is handed ( CallbackInfo , CallbackInfoReturnable ), with Mixin's public names. dev/rustyminecraft/java/ : the layer's internals: Host (natives into the game), Objects (the objects a hook point hands a handler), GameRegistry , Layer (the mods' class loader, entry points, measurements) and fabric/ (events the game fires, the loader's answers). Members named rm$... are the layer's own (binding an object to the game's handle, describing a registration); no mod calls them.

x: Tick counter: the Java layer's test mod A Fabric mod for 26.3, written for this repository: TickMixin counts server ticks from an @Inject at the start of MinecraftServer.tickServer , reads the server's tick count through a @Shadow method, and cancels the tick when asked to. MiningMixin doubles the mining progress with a @ModifyReturnValue on BlockBehaviour.getDestroyProgress , and reads its arguments (the block state, the player, the level, the position) and this (the block). The tests ( tests/jvm.rs ) and examples/jvm_cost.rs compile it with the JDK's javac into a jar, against the Java layer's own classes ( java/ : the API layer with vanilla's names, Fabric API's facade, Mixin's CallbackInfo ) and stubs/ : the Mixin and MixinExtras annotations it uses, written here (names and members from their public documentation). h: Owner updates · Running it
x: horizon-mod-registry The service behind the registry's submission form ( playhorizon.dev/mods/submit ). A creator signs in with GitHub and lists a project by its GitHub repository and a page ( repo plus name, summary, licence...): the service checks that the repository is public and opens a pull request adding mods/<id>.toml to horizon-rust/horizon-mods , where a reviewer reads the repository once. It takes no versions for such a project : they are the repository's GitHub releases, read and checked by that repository's CI with no pull request ("publish a GitHub release in ", a 409). Projects listed before that (no repo ) can still be sent as a file: the service runs the file's own checks ( horizon_mods::index::inspect , the signature, the entry's fields), uploads it to the staging release as <sha256>.<extension> and opens a pull request adding or updating the entry. Formats and rules: docs/api/mod-index.md . Signed-in players also rate published projects, 1 to 5 stars: one rating per GitHub account and project, which they can change, never their own project's. That is the only data it keeps, in one SQLite file ( REGISTRY_DB ); it only ever shows totals, never who rated. A session is a signed cookie holding the GitHub login and id, and the user's OAuth token is used once, to read them, and dropped. The sign-in asks for no scope. Route GET /api/mods/auth/login Starts the GitHub sign-in; ?back=/mods/<id> (or /mods ) comes back to that page GET /api/mods/auth/callback GitHub's redirect: sets the session, back to /mods/submit or the back page POST /api/mods/auth/logout Ends it GET /api/mods/me {login, csrf} , or 401 POST /api/mods/submit Multipart: entry (JSON: id kind name summary description authors license icon key , and either repo (no file: lists the project) or source signature version game changelog with the file (a project with no repo )); {pull_request} or {error} GET /api/mods/ratings {projects: {<id>: {average, count}}} for every rated project; cached a minute GET /api/mods/<id>/rating The signed-in account's own {stars} (null when it hasn't rated), or 401 POST /api/mods/<id>/rating JSON {stars} , 1 to 5: sets or changes it; {stars, average, count} or {error} GET /healthz ok A submission or a rating must come from REGISTRY_PUBLIC_URL 's origin with the session's X-CSRF-Token . Six submissions per account and sixty in all per hour; thirty ratings per account and 600 in all. A project's owners can't rate it, and only projects on the registry's main can be rated. Only an entry's owners publish its updates; a key change, an icon in the repository or anything else is a pull request by hand. Owner updates Only for projects with no repo (a project listed by its repository has no update to send). A reviewer's approval is not needed for an owner update : the submitter's login is in the entry's owners on the registry's main , and the only change to the entry is one new version (key, owners, icon, kind, id, name, summary, description, authors, licence

x: horizon-telemetry-server This server receives what players choose to send (performance summaries, crash and bug reports, benchmark uploads: docs/telemetry.md ) and stores it in one SQLite file. It serves anonymous totals to the website. It also keeps the live player count from the games' anonymous "I'm playing" pings, in memory only, and takes what players send from the hub (playhorizon.dev/hub): votes and bug reports. Endpoints POST /v1/batch A zstd batch ( Content-Encoding: zstd , at most 256 KiB, 1 MiB inflated, 64 items). Returns 204. Returns 400 for a bad batch, 413 for one too large, 415 if it is not zstd, 429 when over a limit. DELETE /v1/installs/<id> Deletes everything that install sent. x: Animated sprite mip cache animate_sprites retains full mip chains for previously displayed source frames. The renderer owns an immutable snapshot of animations, size and mip settings; resource reload replaces that snapshot and drops its cache. Mipmap options only change the sampled view, so the full chains stay valid. Frame selection, skipped unchanged frames, upload order and mip bytes are preserved. Admission is lazy, with an 8 MiB limit on retained Vec capacities and a separate 4,096-entry limit on map metadata. The existing fixed integer hasher avoids consuming random seeds for cache bookkeeping. An admitted frame stays until resource reload; a frame that does not fit uses the original generation path. There is no eviction churn. These limits apply to the additional cache, excluding the existing source frames and the original generator's temporary allocations. Map/allocator overhead is additional and bounded by the entry limit. Reproduce Use prepared 26.3 resources at .local/horizon-client/26.3 . All block/item textures are loaded, including static layers that set the shared array size (the 64px straw-bed texture). h: How a check acts · Checks · Writing a check
x: The dedicated server's anticheat Rusty Minecraft's dedicated server can check what players send beyond what vanilla checks. It is off : a server that doesn't turn it on runs vanilla's checks only ("moved too quickly", "moved wrongly"...) and costs nothing more. An owner turns it on in server.toml : [anticheat] enabled = true alerts = true # tell online operators (alert_level, default 2) in their chat alert_level = 2 log = "logs/anticheat.log" # every flag, one line each; "" writes none [anticheat.timer] # each check has a table like this one; every key is optional enabled = true setback = 2 alert = 5 kick = 20 decay = 0.02 It lives in the server for now, in its own crate ( horizon-anticheat ) plus one file of the hub ( lan/anticheat.rs ), because the native mod API ( native-mods.md ) has no hooks yet for a player's moves (the position, the on-ground claim, cancelling a move) or for packet timing. It moves into a native mod once those hooks exist. horizon-server checks the section before every start; the game reads it from server.toml when it starts ( horizon-client --dedicated run by hand reads the same file from its folder, if there is one). How a check acts A check that fails flags the player: the check's violation level (VL) rises (by 1 for most flags) and falls back by decay every second. From setback on, the move or action is cancelled and the player is put back where the server last had them; from alert on, the console, the log and the online operators are told (at most once a second per player and check); from kick on, the player is disconnected with "Kicked by the server's anticheat". A threshold at 0 turns that action off. Nothing bans: the owner reads the log and decides. Every flag goes to log , with the time, the player, the check, its level, what it saw and what was done: [2026-10-30 17:29:55] Steve failed timer (VL 5.9): 301 ms ahead, sent back Checks Check Catches How timer a sped-up game (more ticks a second than the server's clock) vanilla's client ends each tick with ServerboundClientTickEndPacket, at the server's tick rate. Each one spends one tick of a balance that wall-clock time fills. A client more than tolerance_ms (300) ahead is flagged; a quiet connection banks at most max_lag_ms (1000), so a lag spike's backlog isn't flagged and a pause can't be saved for a burst. A slow server tick adds its own time before its backlog is counted. ground no-fall (claiming the ground to skip fall damage) and walking on water a move that says it ends on the ground is judged only when every block around the feet (0.6 below them, 1/16 wider than the body) is air or a fluid, nothing collides a tenth of a block down, and no boat, minecart, shulker or happy ghast is near. Anything else (powder snow, scaffolding, a waterlogged slab...) isn't judged. A false claim is always dropped, so vanilla's fall damage follows; creative, spectators and gliders are skipped (no fall damage to dodge). prediction (being built) speed, step, fly, jesus: any move

x: Rusty Minecraft APIs Rusty Minecraft has seven surfaces that other programs and people build on. Each one has an API (the contract: what you may call, read or write, and what Rusty Minecraft promises about it) and an SDK (the tools that help you use it). This section has one page per surface, plus the rules every surface follows: stability and versioning . Surface For API today Stability Reference Mods mod authors content mods: manifest api 0.2; native mods: a horizon-mixins bundle ( native-mods.md ) preview (content), experimental (native) mods.md Shaders shader authors none yet: packs were removed on 2026-10-24 planned none Agent control agents, scripts, tests horizon-ctl , its MCP server, the game's control socket preview horizon-ctl-commands.md (generated) Servers hosts, panels, bots horizon-server commands, server.toml , control API /api/v1 stable server-reference.md (generated) Launcher players' agents, pack makers horizon-launcher commands and its MCP server preview launcher-commands.md (generated) Launch other launchers horizon-client 's launch options, the session JSON, exit codes experimental launch-reference.md (generated) Data formats tools that read Rusty Minecraft's files benchmark reports, telemetry, settings files, signed checksums stable or preview, per format on that page How these APIs are designed From the people who use them. Each API starts from what a mod author, a pack author, a server host or an agent needs to do, written down as tasks ("a host backs up the world from a script"), and from how Rusty Minecraft is built: Rust, wgpu and a server thread that runs every world. A function exists because a task needs it. Our own design. Rusty Minecraft's APIs are not modelled on any other project's. Contributors may know other mod loaders, renderers and server platforms exist, but their source and API references are never read, copied or paraphrased here, and our names, shapes and docs are not taken from theirs. Vanilla Minecraft 26.3 is the reference for game concepts: ids, commands, server.properties , data packs and resource packs. Safe by default. A content mod is data and runs no code; a native mod runs with the player's rights, so it is off by default, behind a warning and reviewed before the registry lists it; the control sockets listen on this computer only, behind a token; nothing here is on by default where it would change vanilla's look or behaviour. Free when unused. An API nobody uses costs nothing per tick or per frame: no engine, no thread, no allocation. One contract for every mode. In-frame single player, the server thread, LAN and the dedicated server run the same gameplay code ( AGENTS.md ), so a server-side API serves all of them. x: Shader API Rusty Minecraft has no shader packs today: the earlier implementation was removed on 2026-10-24. Two things will replace it, designed separately: a Rusty Minecraft shader API , described here, and a clean-room loader for the existing pack format (its own spec; it is not part of this API). Both sit on the same renderer hooks, agreed between the two. Overview: what a shader author will be able to do Write WGSL against documented stages of Rusty Minecraft's renderer, with typed inputs, options the player can change, a reload as soon as a file is saved and an overlay that shows what each pass costs and draws. The renderer keeps everything that makes it fast (culling, batching, LOD, the mesher); a pack changes how surfaces and light look, not how the world is fed to the GPU. The design A pack is a folder or a zip with horizon-shaders.toml (id, name, version, the api line, the stages it uses, its options) and WGSL files. No preprocessor and no other shading language: WGSL is what wgpu validates and compiles for Vulkan, Metal and DirectX 12. Stages, not pipelines. A stage is a function with a fixed signature that the renderer calls inside its own pass, for example a terrain material ( fn material(input: TerrainInput) -> Surface ), the lighting of the visible surfaces, the sky, an optional shadow pass, and a chain of full-screen post passes ending in the frame. A pack that leaves a stage out gets vanilla's look for it. Typed inputs. Each stage receives structs (the frame: time, camera, sun and moon, weather, fog; the surface: position, normal, block and its light) whose WGSL is generated from the Rust types the renderer uploads. The generated reference lists every field with its unit and range, and a test fails when it drifts. Options are WGSL override constants. The manifest declares each option (on/off, a number in a range, a choice) with its default; the game shows them on the pack's settings screen and sets them when it builds the pipeline. No text substitution, and every option combination is validated the same way. Hot reload. The game watches the pack's folder. A saved file is validated with naga and the stage rebuilt; on an error the last good version keeps drawing and the error, with its file and line, is shown in the overlay. Debug overlay. GPU time per stage and pass (timestamp queries), the targets each pass writes (show any of them full-screen), the pack's options and its compile errors. Budgets. A pack declares the targets and passes it needs; the renderer refuses more than its limits, and the benchmark ( benchmark-report.md ) records the pack and its cost, so "fast" stays measured. Off by default. Without a pack the renderer is vanilla's look, and no pack code runs. The pack format (schema 1) A pack is a folder, or the same files zipped as a .hshader , with horizon-shaders.toml at its root (crate horizon-shader-api ; the sample with every key is crates/horizon-shader-api/tests/samples/schema-1/ ): schema = 1 # the manifest's for

x: API stability and versioning The rules every Rusty Minecraft API follows ( the APIs ): how each one is versioned, what the stability levels promise, how something is deprecated and removed, and the tests that keep old mods, scripts and tools working. Versions Each API has its own version , separate from the game's release ( v0.2.14 , versioning.md ) and from Minecraft's. A game release says which API versions it serves. Semantic versioning , MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH . A line is what stays compatible: 0.1 , 0.2 , … before 1.0, then 1 , 2 , …. Before 1.0: an addition makes the next patch ( 0.1.0 → 0.1.1 ); a breaking change starts the next line ( 0.2.0 ). From 1.0: an addition makes the next minor ( 1.0 → 1.1 ); a breaking change starts the next major ( 2.0 ). Where the version lives: API The version A user names the line they need Content mods the manifest's api line api = "0.2" in horizon-mod.toml Native mods the Rusty Minecraft and horizon-mixins revisions the bundle pins horizon_revision in horizon-mixin.toml Agent control the control protocol's version (planned: a hello reply and MCP serverInfo ) horizon-ctl --api 1 (planned) Server control API the path ( /api/v1/ ) the path server.toml the file's keys; a key is never renamed in place nothing: old files keep loading Launcher commands the command names and their --json output nothing Data formats a version or schema field in the file the reader rejects versions newer than it knows What counts as a breaking change Breaking: removing or renaming anything; changing a type, a default, a unit or a meaning; making something optional required; refusing input that was accepted; a JSON field that changes type. Not breaking: a new function, interface, capability, command, endpoint, tool or server.toml key; a new optional argument or JSON field (readers must ignore fields they don't know); faster, or fixing behaviour to what the reference already says. Stability levels Every part of an API has one level, shown in its reference and its surface page. Experimental Preview Stable Who may use it opt-in only (a flag or a manifest field naming it); never in a release default anyone; marked "preview" where players see it (a mod's row on the Mods page) anyone May change in any release, without notice only at a new line, after a deprecation only at a new major, after a deprecation Deprecation window none at least 30 days, with one release line serving old and new at least 180 days, with the old major served beside the new one Needs a design note a generated reference, a guide section, an example, compatibility tests the same, plus one line of real use without a break Promotion. Experimental → preview when it has what the table asks. Preview → stable when real users (a published mod, a host's script, an agent's tool) used it for a whole line and nothing broke. h: What is measured · How it is kept fair · Known caveats · Benchmark your own machine · Reproduce it · Results
x: Benchmark: Rusty Minecraft vs vanilla 26.3 tools/perf_bench.py measures Rusty Minecraft, the vanilla 26.3 client and vanilla with performance mods on the same machine, the same world and the same camera path, and computes every number with the same code. This page says what it measures, how it keeps the comparison fair, what it can't control, and how to reproduce it. The results are in Results . What is measured One game is started per window size (1280x720 and 1920x1080 by default) and render distance (8, 16 and 32 chunks by default), each from a fresh world, so nothing generated by an earlier run is reused. In each game: Start to the title screen. Wall-clock time from starting the process to the first frame of the title screen with no loading overlay. Create the world. A creative world named PerfBench , seed 1234, default world type and difficulty, created the way the game's own Create World does. Start to in-world is the time from starting the process until the player has spawned and every chunk around the spawn is loaded and drawn. Four scenes , the paths of tools/graphics_bench.py : straight 192-block flights over a village, a forest, the ocean and a mountain. For each scene the player is teleported to the start (time set to noon), held there flying, and the chunk load time is the time from the teleport until every chunk in view distance is loaded and drawn. After 2 seconds of settling, the player flies the path at constant speed in 12 seconds (16 blocks per second, faster than sprint-flying), facing along it at the scene's pitch, placed on the line every frame. Chunks are generated and drawn as they come into range during the flight, as in play. Frame times. Every frame of every flight is recorded (time between the starts of consecutive frames). From them: average FPS, 1% and 0.1% lows (the average frame time of the slowest 1% or 0.1% of frames, as FPS: a single long freeze shows), the median, p95, p99 and p99.9 frame times, the slowest frame, and the share of frames in buckets (under 4.17 ms = 240 FPS, 8.33, 16.67, 33.33, 50, 100 ms, and over). Memory. The process's resident set size (RSS), sampled 4 times a second from outside the process ( ps on macOS and Linux, the working set, as Task Manager shows it, on Windows): peak over the whole run (startup included) and steady , the median during the flights. For vanilla this counts the whole JVM (heap, JIT, native buffers, the integrated server), for Rusty Minecraft the whole process. GPU memory where it can be read: Rusty Minecraft's own Vulkan allocator total, and what nvidia-smi attributes to the process on NVIDIA. On Apple Silicon the GPU shares RAM and no per-process figure is available. How it is kept fair Same machine, same run conditions. Games run one at a time; the load average before and after each run (Windows has none, so it is left out there) and the machine (CPU, RAM, OS) are stored with the results. x: Biome lookup Rusty Minecraft implements Java Edition 26.3 block-to-quart biome lookup. BiomeZoom accepts the obfuscated biome seed and chooses among eight jittered quart corners in vanilla order, retaining strict distance ties and signed coordinate wrapping. The caller resolves the selected quart coordinate through its biome provider. Direct noise-biome queries bypass this selection and shift block coordinates; floating-point positions are floored with Java's saturating integer conversion. obfuscate_seed computes the vanilla SHA-256 transform of the little-endian world seed and reads the first eight digest bytes as a little-endian signed long. The core keeps a fixed-input implementation without adding runtime dependencies. Run python3 tools/test_biome_zoom_parity.py . The local report records 256,933 matching lines per reference JAR : 4,104 seed hashes , 169,408 block queries and 83,421 floating-position queries . Actual vanilla BiomeManager methods call a traced resolver; the suite compares selected quart coordinates, direct queries and source replacement retaining the same zoom seed. Seed hashes also match Python hashlib independently. The corpus includes dense neighborhoods, negative quart boundaries, both signed integer extremes, distant coordinates, randomized seeds/positions, and double NaNs, infinities and subnormals. Source and fixture hashes are captured, changes during validation invalidate the result, and reference artifacts stay private. CI includes the comparison; remote outcomes have not been observed. This validates coordinate selection, not biome storage, biome-source generation, chunk blending, or complete generated worlds. Chunk biome storage BiomeChunk<T> stores each section's 64 quart-resolution biome values. Reads clamp quart Y to the chunk and wrap quart X/Z into its local grid. Fills visit sections bottom to top and query each section in X/Y/Z order. Each completed section is committed; a resolver failure retains the failing section's previous values. Inclusive generation bounds select all intersecting sections. Run python3 tools/test_biome_chunk_parity.py . The local chunk report records 478,340 matching lines per reference JAR across 20 fixtures and 160 fills , including 21,120 quart-biome queries . Native ProtoChunk and LevelChunkSection methods supply the reference behavior. Tests use synthetic holder identities, up to 512 distinct values, repeated fills, provider failures at calls 0/63/64/65, generation bounds cutting through sections, and the complete supported aligned vertical range. The reference chunk is at BIOMES status. This storage uses dense arrays and compares biome values rather than vanilla's internal palette layout. Packet/save integration and chunk lifecycle transitions remain separate work. Clipped generation bounds must remain within the chunk; invalid bounds return an error before mutation. Biome temperatures Rusty Minecraft implements Java Edition 26.3 biome temperature sampling, including the frozen modifier, height adjustment, rain/snow thresholds, precipitation selection and the small frozen-ocean iceberg melt predicate. The fixed seeded simplex and noise-stack sources use the existing Rust noise implementation. BiomeTemperatureSettings supplies the immutable inputs. BiomeTemperature is a per-biome, per-worker cache, corresponding to vanilla's thread-local cache. Its 1,024-entry insertion order does not change on hits. Keys use packed block positions and omit sea level, preserving both coordinate aliases and cached results across sea-level changes. x: Carving Rusty Minecraft implements Java Edition 26.3 carving-mask storage and traversal. CarvingMask packs cells in Y/Z/X order into 64-bit words. Its column iterator finds contiguous marked runs and splits them into inclusive vertical intervals, using word scans without allocating a list of individual cells or columns. try_visit_mut retains vanilla callback behavior: adding cells during traversal changes subsequent run searches, while an already selected run keeps its original boundaries. Callback failures stop immediately and retain prior mutations. Coordinate arithmetic wraps like Java, including positive out-of-range aliases; negative indices return an error. Rusty Minecraft collision geometry The version target is Minecraft Java Edition 26.3 . Geometry is a simulation foundation; Rusty Minecraft has a native client for inspecting a controlled block scene. Live gameplay and entity simulation remain unfinished. horizon-core::geometry provides Vec3 , Aabb , Axis , Direction , BlockHit , and immutable VoxelShape values. Coordinates are doubles. Arithmetic keeps vanilla's operation order, signed zero, NaN comparisons, normalization threshold, and collision epsilon. It does not enable approximate or fused simulation math. Implemented vector operations include addition/subtraction, vector-to, component products, scaling, normalization, dot/cross products, interpolation, projection, distance/length, horizontal vectors and finite/equality checks. Rotations, look directions, alignment, axis replacement, direction offsets, and pitch/yaw extraction are also implemented. The full Vec3 API and entity integration remain absent. Trig uses vanilla's 65,536-entry float sine table with double angle scaling and Java long narrowing. Offscreen frame compositor Part 1 of the splitscreen series (#3541). The renderer exposes its offscreen frame and can hand its window surface to a compositor on the same GPU device. The compositor clears uncovered pixels to black and copies each BGRA view to its assigned position, clipping at the window edge. Returning the surface through Renderer::take_back lets the next renderer draw on the window again. The normal game path does not create a compositor. A standalone example exercises this without game resources, profiles, audio or launcher data: cargo run --profile fast -p horizon-client-render --example compositor cargo run --profile fast -p horizon-client-render --example compositor -- --smoke The window shows a red view on the left and a blue one on the right. Resize it to check clipping and uncovered black regions. The smoke run presents 20 frames, switches vsync off, tests zero and oversized dimensions, resizes the window, then exits. Unsupported surface copy formats return an error. Unit coverage checks clipping while a view still has its old size during a resize.

Neighboring model-face visibility horizon-world::block_render::FaceVisibility decides whether to emit a model quad with a culling direction beside a neighboring block. It prepares immutable face geometry from the pinned raw occlusion shapes, shares faces across states, and caches shape-pair subtraction with bounded memory. The development client now uses it for resident chunk model meshing, including cross-chunk neighbors. The decision preserves the native order: a canonical full neighbor face hides the quad, block-specific suppression can hide it, canonical empty faces bypass the shape comparison, and partial faces use ONLY_FIRST subtraction. Full occlusion is computed from geometry, independently of collision or support. Block-specific suppression covers every method owner in the pinned registry: ordinary blocks, same-block glass/ice and powder snow, bars/panes, leaves, liquids, and mangrove roots. Bars respect the loaded bars tag, facing connections, and the neighbor's boolean property availability. Leaf suppression is controlled by the cutout-leaves setting. Liquids compare fluid families, including contained water in waterlogged neighbors. Mangrove roots suppress vertical internal faces. The native comparison calls actual BlockState.skipRendering and Block.shouldRenderFace with pinned tags bound in both reference JARs. It covers all 35,723 states and 1,286 block definitions: 1,441,816 ordered state pairs, six directions and two leaf settings (17,301,792 direction/setting cases). Every overriding family has exhaustive same-block state pairs; bars and panes also have exhaustive cross-material connection pairs. Representative and seeded random neighbors exercise partial occlusion across the rest of the registry. Heightmaps Rusty Minecraft implements the six heightmap types in the pinned Minecraft Java Edition 26.3 . Each map stores 256 relative column heights in padded 64-bit words. World-surface predicates use isAir ; ocean-floor predicates use the version's blocks_motion_in_heightmap block tag. Motion-blocking maps also include nonempty fluid states, with the separate no-leaves tag for that variant. HeightmapState supplies block behavior and tag membership. HeightmapChunk supplies the vertical extent, highest occupied section and block reads. The map owns its packed data and checks that a supplied chunk has the same bounds. Its current constructor accepts positive, aligned ranges within the vanilla noise settings codec domain; zero-height and arbitrary runtime accessors are outside this bounded API. Updates retain the early return for blocks below the top two positions. Removing a qualifying surface scans downward until another qualifying block is found. Priming scans X, then Z, then descending Y, sharing each block read across the selected maps. It skips exact AIR blocks and stops a column when all selected maps have found a surface. If a column finds nothing, its existing value remains. This also applies to re-priming after a raw-data length mismatch. Raw imports preserve every bit when the word count matches, including padding, unused slots and values above the build height. Column addressing retains Java's wrapped x + z * 16 calculation; invalid final indices return typed errors. The Rust API does not expose a mutable alias to its internal words. It covers all 35,723 block states , all six predicate and persistence/client flags, and 100 chunk fixtures with 86,806 state writes, 54,306 column queries, 516 priming calls, 378 raw-data loads and additional update-only error cases. Selected fixtures compare exact ordered block reads. Cases include section and vertical bounds, leaves, fluid-bearing states, air variants, removal rescans, empty-column retention, packed padding, invalid raw lengths and wrapped column indices. Air/fluid facts and state identities are exported independently from each JAR and required to agree. These are private test inputs, not ports of block behavioral methods. Rust resolves heightmap tag membership using its tag loader and the 300 bundled block-tag resources. The reference binds those resources to the actual vanilla block registry and invokes Heightmap on ProtoChunk instances. Only in-memory section storage is used; placeholder biome holders do not exercise biome properties or section codecs. Source and fixture changes during a run invalidate its report. Before you start Online mode checks accounts (release v2026.10.17.07 and newer). With online_mode = true , the default, players who sign in with the official Minecraft launcher join with their own accounts, as on a vanilla server. Names you add are accounts (release v2026.10.17.14 and newer). init --player , horizon-server whitelist add and op , and the console's whitelist add , op and ban look a name up the way vanilla does: players already seen (kept in usercache.json ), then Mojang's profile service. x: How Rusty Minecraft is built Who writes Rusty Minecraft, how changes are checked, and why it is safe to run. You can check every claim on this page in the repository, and anything not done yet is marked as not done. This page is also on the website: playhorizon.dev/docs/how-horizon-is-built . The longer version, with what is still missing, is Security . Who builds it Rusty Minecraft is Ludovic Marie's project: he decides what it does and what ships. Most of the code is written by AI agents : Claude sessions that Ludovic runs, and contributors' own AI tools. Some contributors write their code by hand. Agents say what they are. A pull request opened by one of Ludovic's agents starts with "Opened by Ludovic's AI agent (Claude), not by Ludovic himself.", its comments start with "🤖 Agent:", and its commits name the agent in a Co-Authored-By line. How changes are checked Not every line is read by a person. Instead, every change is checked against the real game, automatically: Harnesses. A harness is a test that gives the same inputs to Rusty Minecraft and to the real Minecraft 26.3, then compares the results. There are 326 of them (25 October 2026), from world generation to mobs, redstone and commands. The status table shows what they cover. Passing them all does not prove that nothing else differs. Checks on every pull request. verify runs on GitHub's machines for every pull request and every change to main: formatting, lints with warnings treated as errors, the tests, and the check that no Minecraft files are committed. Main takes no change without it. parity runs the harnesses a change can affect, on a machine that holds a copy of Minecraft. For a pull request from a fork, it runs once a maintainer has read the change. Outside contributions are checked again. Before a contributor's pull request merges, Ludovic's agents compare what it claims with vanilla's own code, review it line by line, rewrite the weak parts, and test it in single player, on a LAN and on a dedicated server where those apply. Releases are tested first. A release is published only after its smoke test passes (the game starts and draws a world) and while no issue is labelled release-blocker . Why it's safe to run Open source. All of the code is public on GitHub , under the MIT licence. Built from the public code. Releases are built by GitHub Actions, the build service of GitHub, from the public source. Linux and Windows are built on GitHub's machines, and macOS on Ludovic's Mac mini, which runs GitHub Actions jobs. Every build log is public . Signed checksums. Every release has a SHA256SUMS file, a fingerprint of each download, and SHA256SUMS.sig , a signature of that list made with Rusty Minecraft's release key, which only release builds from main can use. The launcher and horizon-server update check both before they install anything, and refuse a file that does not match. These primitives now feed the chunk surface stage . ClayBands generates all 192 entries from the supplied clay-band random stream. It preserves orange placement, colored-band widths and overwrites, white/gray adjacency checks and conditional random draws. MaterialSurface derives that stream from the world's root positional factory using minecraft:clay_bands . Its surface-depth query uses a fresh position-derived random stream. Band lookup rounds the float noise offset with Java's tie and saturation rules, then uses wrapped integer addition and signed remainder. x: Rusty Minecraft native client horizon-client is the playable Rust client for Minecraft Java Edition 26.3. It streams a world around the player on worker threads, renders every vanilla block model with smooth lighting and biome tints, and runs the validated player physics, health and hunger at 20 ticks per second. You can mine with vanilla hardness/tool rules, collect drops from the block loot tables, place blocks, craft in the 2x2 inventory grid or on a crafting table, and save and reload worlds in vanilla's Anvil format. Status: playable; players get it through the launcher . The Java parity table in the README scores each subsystem against vanilla and lists what is still missing; Rust rewrite status has the details. A checkout never downloads the game: resource preparation imports your own copy (the 26.3 client from your official launcher install, and the 26.3 server jar you downloaded yourself; see Build from source ), verifies it against the pinned checksums, runs vanilla's data generator and small exporters against those jars, and extracts the jar's assets and data into ignored .local/horizon-client/26.3/ . x: Native hook points, modelled on NeoForge 26.3 (proposal) Status: proposal, for the authors of hook PRs to comment on. Nothing here is built yet. Checked against native-hooks.json on main (41 hooks, NATIVE_HOOKS_API 24) on 31 October 2026. Native mods hook empty functions in crates/horizon-client/src/game/native_hooks.rs , listed by name in native-hooks.json ( native-mods.md ). So far each hook was designed on its own, and open PRs number their API versions over each other. This proposes one reference for every new hook point: the NeoForge 26.3 event that does the same thing. Why NeoForge: Its events already answer the questions each of our hooks asks again: where exactly it fires, on which side, what it can cancel, what it is handed. Mod authors know them. A Java mod's @SubscribeEvent methods map to hook names, which helps porting by hand. horizon-port-pack may suggest mappings for a human to review, not translate listeners automatically. What we take is event names and their documented contracts, from NeoForge's public user documentation ( https://docs.neoforged.net/ ) only, each claim below citing the page it comes from, as CONTRIBUTING.md allows. Nobody reads, copies, translates or paraphrases NeoForge's source, its patches included: where a hook fires is decided from vanilla 26.3's own methods, and the hooks stay Rusty Minecraft's own Rust. Rules Name. A hook with a NeoForge counterpart takes the event's name in snake case, its nested class included: ServerTickEvent.Pre → server_tick_pre , function native_server_tick_pre ; PlayerInteractEvent.RightClickBlock → right_click_block . A hook with no counterpart (the minimap, the mods list, the item panel) keeps a Rusty Minecraft name. Firing point. It fires in Rusty Minecraft's port of the vanilla method where the documented event happens (the tick starts, a block is broken), at the point vanilla's own steps make that true. The catalog names the vanilla method, so a reviewer can check it with tools/rea_vanilla.py . Side. NeoForge documents that "some events are only fired on one side" ( Events , "Sided Events"); the rest fire on whichever side runs the method. Rusty Minecraft has one binary with several Game s (the window, the server thread, a dedicated server), so each hook says its side: server : the server's Game (single player's server thread, LAN host, dedicated) and the in-frame path. client : the window's Game . both : both, with the Game 's role available ( native_window ). Interactions are both : the client predicts, the server acts, and a mod that claims a use on one side only gets the two out of step. Cancel and results. Hooks never return; several mods hook the same point. A cancellable event takes canceled: &mut bool ; one with a result (an InteractionResult ) takes result: &mut Option<...> . Every mod is called; a mod checks *canceled itself when it should stand back. NeoForge's handlers likewise "can opt to explicitly receive cancelled events" and some events implement ICancellableE

x: Rusty Minecraft noise-generation scope The target is the repository-pinned Minecraft Java Edition 26.3 . The Rust samplers live in crates/horizon-core/src/noise/ and use the checked legacy or xoroshiro streams. They are a world-generation foundation; Rusty Minecraft does not yet generate complete vanilla chunks or run a playable Rust game. Implemented behavior Gradient offsets and all 256 permutation entries, including the three random draws consumed when simplex offsets are disabled. 26.3 Perlin 2D/3D sampling, single-precision interpolation and accumulation into caller-supplied derivative arrays. Smeared Perlin uses its adjusted Y component for gradient dots and the original component for interpolation. Its inherited derivative method samples the unsmeared field. Simplex 2D/3D sampling with both offset modes, double-precision corner arithmetic and single-precision return values. The second 2D coordinate uses the Y offset. Normal coordinate wrapping with the Far Lands debug flag disabled, including the fast-path boundary immediately below 2^24. Positive strided density volumes with Z/X/Y flat ordering, Java-wrapping block coordinates, bulk Perlin/smeared-Perlin gradient reuse, scalar simplex volumes, repeated scaled accumulation and untouched buffer tails. Ordered noise stacks, nested sampling, flattened stack composition, layer access and range arithmetic. Zero-amplitude layers are retained. Flattening rescales each layer before sampling and can differ from a nested stack. Normal-noise octave selection, frequencies, amplitude modifiers, compensated amplitude sums, enabled/disabled/legacy normalization and the parity factory. Modern creation forks two positional factories and derives each octave from its name, then interleaves the two sets of Perlin layers. Legacy Nether biome initialization, including reverse octave construction, exactly 262 integer draws for skipped octaves, rejected positive octaves and the RNG state left by initialization failures. Its two stacks are flattened in sequence, preserving their distinct accumulation order. The bulk Perlin kernel adds X/Z gradient contributions before Y. Calling the scalar sampler repeatedly would rearrange those operations and can change the result. Rust preserves the bulk path and caches its eight gradients while the Y cell remains unchanged. These are implementation choices checked for behavior; no whole-game frame-rate or generation-speed improvement has been measured. Validation After preparing the pinned artifacts with python3 tools/lab.py prepare , run: cargo test --workspace cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings python3 tools/test_noise_parity.py The original Java adapter invokes the actual downloaded classes on both client and server JARs. It exposes offsets, permutations, octave parameters and layer weights for comparison, and calls the reference scalar and bulk methods. Artifacts and dependencies are authenticated against the repository lock and the official bundled chec

x: For server owners: server.properties to server.toml You run a vanilla server today and edit server.properties . With horizon-server you edit one file, server.toml , instead. Before every start the server writes server.properties from it, so the game reads exactly what a vanilla server reads. This page maps one to the other. The full guide is hosting.md ; the design is server.md , section 4. Moving over Run horizon-server init in your server folder, or horizon-server import server.properties . It reads the file with vanilla's own parser: keys that have a field below go into their section of server.toml ; any other key that differs from vanilla's default goes into [properties] ; keys left at their defaults are dropped, so the file stays short; your original is kept as server.properties.imported . The world folder, ops.json , whitelist.json , the ban lists and usercache.json keep vanilla's names and formats, so going back to a vanilla server works too. Keys that have a field server.properties server.toml Default motd [server] motd "A Minecraft Server" server-port [server] port 25565 server-ip [server] bind "" (every address) max-players [server] max_players 20 online-mode [server] online_mode true white-list [server] whitelist true enforce-whitelist [server] enforce_whitelist false view-distance [server] view_distance 10 simulation-distance [server] simulation_distance 10 level-name [world] name "world" level-seed [world] seed "" (random on first start) gamemode [world] game_mode "survival" difficulty [world] difficulty "easy" hardcore [world] hardcore false Two details differ from vanilla's file: white-list becomes whitelist , and a seed may be a number or any text (vanilla hashes text), written as a string. Every other key Put any other vanilla key under [properties] , spelled as vanilla spells it: [properties] spawn-protection = 16 resource-pack = "https://example.com/pack.zip" A key that has a field above is an error under [properties] ; set it in its section. Settings that are not in server.properties These belong to horizon-server , not to the game: server.toml Meaning [engine] path , resources , restart_on_crash Which game program and prepared files to run, and whether to restart it after a crash. [backups] every , keep Automatic backups ( "6h" , "0" turns them off) and how many to keep. [updates] keep Other releases kept besides the one in use and the one rollback goes to. [panel] bind , allow_public The web panel's address ( "" turns it off) and whether it may listen on a public address. What to know when you switch Edit server.toml , not server.properties . The latter is rewritten at every start. Mistakes stop the start. Unknown keys and values vanilla would refuse are errors, not ignored. In-game changes survive. When the game changes a setting itself ( /whitelist on ), the supervisor copies it back into server.toml after the game stops, and keeps your comments and order. Changes apply at the next restart. horizon-server config set KEY=VA

Running the vanilla harnesses tools/parity.py runs the tools/test_*_parity.py harnesses in parallel and reruns only what a change can affect: python3 tools/parity.py # harnesses whose inputs changed, or that never passed python3 tools/parity.py food light # these harnesses, whatever their state python3 tools/parity.py --failed # the ones that failed last time python3 tools/parity.py --all # everything, from scratch: the audit (26 minutes on the Mac mini alone) python3 tools/parity.py --fresh food # don't reuse vanilla oracle results python3 tools/parity.py --repeat 3 food # run it three times; the runs must agree python3 tools/parity.py --hosts macmini,playhorizon # with other machines (default: tools/parity_hosts.json's default list, empty) python3 tools/parity.py --list # what would run python3 tools/parity.py --status # last result of each harness python3 tools/parity.py --changed origin/main # those a branch's changes can affect (CI's parity job) python3 tools/parity.py --changed-files paths.txt # the same for listed paths, in a copy without Git (tools/pr_ready.py) On CI, a pull request runs the parity job only when it changes a harness, an oracle, a probe or the runner; everything else is checked on main by parity-main , a batch of merges at a time, which bisects a failure to the merge that caused it ( tools/parity_main.py ; release-flow.md ). x: Paletted container access The unpack / get cell reader and BlockSection::get / set are hot in the chunk workers: light and mesh workers unpack a section's 4,096 cells before propagating or meshing, and world-generation workers write one block at a time through BlockSection::set . The write path resolved the old cell and probed the palette three times; the bulk readers dispatched the palette per cell; and the storage layer revalidated indices and values a section had already checked. All three are addressed. Changes BlockSection::set ( crates/horizon-world/src/chunk.rs ) previously resolved the old cell through get and then probed the section's palette map three times for one non-trivial write: once to key the old state by id ( local_ids[&old] ), once to test the incoming state ( contains_key ), and once to find it ( get ). The slot at the written index already is the old state's id, so the old state is now read straight from storage, and the incoming state is resolved with a single map probe. The palette-reuse, free-slot and growth paths are unchanged, so the encoded palette, counts, free list and NBT output stay identical. BlockSection::get and set validate the section index and the state id once, then read and write through PackedStorage::read / write ( crates/horizon-core/src/storage.rs ). These skip the storage-level bounds and value checks and the Result that PackedStorage::get / set keep for external callers: a section index is below 4,096 and a palette id always fits the width bits_for_palette chose. Both new methods debug_assert their contract and are used for the hot read, the hot write and the palette-growth re-encode. PalettedContainer::unpack and unpack_u16 ( crates/horizon-core/src/paletted.rs ) matched on the palette variant inside the per-cell loop. Single , List and Global are now dispatched once before the loop, leaving each arm a branch-free indexed loop. No allocation, layout or wire format changes. x: Play with friends A player opens their single-player world to friends with one click and gets an invite code . Friends paste the code (in game: the title screen's Friends button opens Join a Friend, and Direct Connection takes a full code too; or on the launcher's Play page) and join. There is no Rusty Minecraft server in the middle and no account: the code itself says where the host is and holds the key that encrypts the game between them. It is built on Open to LAN: the integrated server ( crates/horizon-client/src/lan ) listens on a local TCP port and speaks the vanilla protocol. Play with friends puts an encrypted tunnel in front of that port. Neither the integrated server nor the guest's client changes: the tunnel carries exactly the bytes vanilla's protocol would send, between a loopback port on each side. guest's game host's game ┌──────────────┐ 127.0.0.1:A ┌────────────┐ TCP, end-to-end encrypted ┌────────────┐ 127.0.0.1:LAN ┌──────────────┐ │ client │────────────▶│ guest │══════════════════════════════▶│ host │──────────────▶│ integrated │ │ (unchanged) │ │ tunnel │ to an address from the code │ tunnel │ │ server (LAN) │ └──────────────┘ └────────────┘ └────────────┘ └──────────────┘ ╲ optional: a relay anyone can run ╱ ╲──────────▶ horizon-relay (short codes, fallback) ◀╱ How it works Hosting. The pause menu's Friends button (vanilla's icon, beside Player Reporting) opens Play with Friends ( friends_screen.rs ); its Start Sharing opens the world to LAN if it isn't (Open to LAN's defaults), then the host's game, on its own: listens on its direct port , TCP 25580 by default (the same port every time, so a port forwarded by hand keeps working; another one if it is taken; HORIZON_FRIENDS_PORT picks it); collects this computer's addresses: the LAN address, VPN addresses (Tailscale's 100.x , ZeroTier and others), IPv6. Container and VM bridges are left out; asks the home router to open the direct port for an hour, renewed every half hour and deleted when sharing stops: PCP (RFC 6887), then NAT-PMP (RFC 6886) on the default gateway, then UPnP IGD (SSDP discovery, SOAP AddPortMapping ). A router that only takes permanent UPnP mappings gets one, deleted on stop the same way (if the game crashes instead, a timed mapping expires within the hour; a permanent one stays until it is removed in the router's settings); asks public STUN servers for its public IPv4 address (only the address: STUN sees UDP, the game is TCP). Defaults: stun.cloudflare.com:3478 and stun.l.google.com:19302 , two independent operators of free STUN at a global scale, so one outage doesn't break discovery. HORIZON_STUN_SERVERS (a comma list, or none ) changes them; builds the invite code : the endpoints (the router mapping, the public address on the direct port, the interface addresses) and a fresh 80-bit secret, in base32 with a checksum. h: How it works
x: Pregeneration: /pregen /pregen generates every chunk of a square or a circle ahead of the players, lights it and saves it, as Chunky does on a Java server. It is Rusty Minecraft's own command (vanilla has none), available in single player with cheats on and to operators (level 2) on a server, from the chat or the server console ( horizon-server cmd pregen start 2500 ). It is off until you turn it on, so /help and the command tree stay vanilla's: a server: horizon-pregen = true under [properties] in server.toml (or horizon-pregen=true in a vanilla folder's server.properties ), then restart it; single player and LAN: start the game with --pregen . /pregen start <radius> [square|circle] [<x> <z>] radius in blocks; the centre defaults to where you stand (the world spawn from the console) /pregen status chunks done, chunks per second, time left /pregen pause | continue stop scheduling new chunks, and go on /pregen cancel stop; what is done stays saved The area is the chunks within radius / 16 chunks of the centre chunk: a square of side 2 * (radius / 16) + 1 (radius 2500 is 313 x 313 = 97,969 chunks), or the chunks whose distance from the centre chunk is at most radius / 16 . It runs in the dimension the command was run in; that level keeps ticking while the task runs, whoever is in it. The progress goes to the server log every five seconds and to the player who started it, and once more when it is done. A task is not kept across a restart: start it again and the chunks already saved load instead of generating. How it works horizon_client::pregen::Pregen cuts the area into strips at most 256 chunks wide and sweeps each north to south with a band of rows ( streaming::Band ) holding about a thousand chunks. Streaming treats the band like a player's area: it generates its chunks and the rings around them that decoration and light need, and lights its own chunks. Once every chunk of the band's first row is lit and post-processed ( LevelChunk.postProcessGeneration , which vanilla runs before a chunk is FULL), the band moves down a row; the rows that fall out of its reach unload and are saved like any chunk the players leave, so memory holds only the rows in flight. The chunks a band reaches are ranked for decoration row by row as they come within its reach ( Streaming::set_band ). Decoration is order dependent where neighbours' writes overlap ( DecorationOrder ), and this makes a task decorate in the same order however its jobs are timed and shared among the workers: the same seed gives the same chunks. Between server ticks the server waits for the workers' results and hands out the next jobs at once ( Streaming::wait , pump_chunks ), instead of once a tick: a chunk passes through five jobs (generate, decorate, finish, light, save), each needing its neighbours' earlier ones. The chunks of the band's outer ring are finished (FULL) but not lit, as at the edge of what a player has loaded; they light when their neighbours load later.

h: An immutable store across releases
x: Resource preparation and filesystem work The reported preparation timings put sounds at 20–29 seconds with little CPU use, versus 0.9–1.4 seconds for fresh client asset extraction. Prefer fewer file opens, reads and writes over parallelizing decompression. Preparation now shares one parsed asset index between panorama, font, pack and language imports. Its destination verification results live only for that preparation. A subsequent invocation checks bytes again, so it can repair corrupt resources. Existing valid destination files do not require the original asset objects to remain installed. A saved asset index also lets preparation preserve full imports when only cached Minecraft JARs remain. New imports are staged beside their destination. On Linux, FICLONE is attempted first; other filesystems fall back to copying while hashing. Cloned copies are hashed before publication. macOS attempts clonefile with the same checked streaming fallback. A whole asset group is staged and verified before any replacement is published; corrupt late panorama faces leave placeholders alone. Temporary files are cleaned up on errors. This is not a transaction for rename failures or process termination during publication: a later run repairs incomplete groups. Unchanged JAR resources are checked by the ZIP member's size and CRC, avoiding repeated decompression. Valid indexed replacements take precedence over JAR placeholders. Reusing checked Minecraft imports also passes the verified artifact/library results directly to the exporters. An immutable store across releases The official launcher's SHA-1 object store already provides an immutable source for indexed assets. Independent filesystem clones let installed Rusty Minecraft releases share physical blocks where supported, without sharing writable inodes. Ordinary copies remain the fallback. A separate Rusty Minecraft store could additionally share complete preparations on filesystems without cloning. Its key would need the pinned client/server hashes, the preparer's output version (or the legacy source/exporter fingerprint), and the actual asset-index digest: Mojang republishes translations without changing the Minecraft release. Two preparations with different optional asset availability must not claim the same complete snapshot. Before adopting that store, separate immutable runtime resources from mutable exporter scratch, classes and logs. Publish snapshots through a temporary directory and atomic rename, give each release an explicit reference, and define locking, corruption repair, migration and garbage collection. Exporters must never receive a shared writable directory or hard-linked files. The existing launcher compatibility check should choose reuse; the store should only supply its bytes. Keep this separate from the open work on output-version compatibility (#1946/#1947). For now, retain independent release directories and clone their resource files. Each sample repeats enough batches for approximately 10 ms of the slower path, capped at 10,000 repetitions; large batches run once. Inputs and outputs pass through black_box . Destruction of outputs is timed. Scope and memory The fixtures cover a 16 by 16 loaded area spanning negative and positive chunks: 3,072 block entities / 768 names for a village and 12,288 / 3,072 for storage. Each chunk has 12 or 48 mixed chests, furnaces and signs, with populated inventories, custom item components, names, saved NBT overlays, saved entity order, and an unmodelled end gateway. h: Behavior · Persistence and use · Validation
x: Rusty Minecraft scheduled ticks The Rust scheduler targets the repository-pinned Minecraft Java Edition 26.3 . It implements scheduled block/fluid queue mechanics and saved tick lists. Actual block/fluid updates, random ticks, block events, neighbor updates, redstone behavior and a running game world remain unimplemented. Behavior horizon_core::ticks supplies TickPriority , ScheduledTick , SavedTick , ChunkTicks and LevelTicks . A numeric TickTypeId represents a registry-owned block or fluid type. Block and fluid scheduling use separate LevelTicks instances. Callers supply identities, game time, sub-tick counters, eligibility, per-call tick limits and behavior callbacks. The first request for a type and position wins, even if a duplicate has an earlier trigger time or a higher priority. A chunk queue orders by signed trigger time, then one of seven priorities, then signed sub-tick order. Once heads are due, different chunks compete by priority and sub-tick order . Consequently, globally sorting every tick by trigger time changes execution. Within the selected chunk, draining stops when its next head loses to the competing chunk head, exceeds the time bound, or exhausts the tick limit. Equal comparator keys follow the pinned Java array heap behavior. Deadline traversal follows the pinned fastutil long-map layout, including resizing, collision shifts and wrapped iterator removals. These details matter when loaded ticks in different chunks share priority and negative sub-tick order. They are covered by differential tests rather than replaced with a new tie breaker. The heap stores tick records inline and retains collection capacity between frames. Area operations probe small chunk grids directly and visit only loaded chunks for large sparse areas, preserving X/Z traversal order. No game FPS or memory gain has been measured. Collection happens before callbacks. A callback can schedule, query, clear, copy, disable or unload chunks; newly scheduled ticks wait for the next collection. has_scheduled covers container queues and pending saved ticks; will_tick_this_tick covers the remaining collected queue. The current callback has already moved to the already-run list. Vanilla's lazily built membership set can remain stale after an area clear; that behavior is preserved until cleanup. Area copying includes already-run, collected and queued ticks and places copied sub-tick orders after the copied source range with wrapping signed-long arithmetic. Disabled chunks retain due entries. Removing a container returns its queue for saving or later reinsertion; collected callbacks still run. Scheduling into an absent chunk returns MissingChunk and does not enqueue. The Rust API adds invariant checks for duplicate chunk insertion, wrong-chunk contents and invalid collection phase transitions. These checks differ from Java's unchecked API and logging, while preserving the tested valid lifecycle. Persistence and use Saved ticks hold a signed 32-bit relative delay. Pack

h: Who does what · What could go wrong before (October 2026) · Where things stand (19 October 2026) · What stops it now · What still needs Ludovic · What this doesn't solve · Reporting a security problem
x: Security How Rusty Minecraft keeps its code and its downloads safe while most of the work is done by AI agents and releases go out by themselves, including when Ludovic isn't at his computer. In plain words: what someone could have done before, what stops them now, and what still needs Ludovic. Who does what Agents (Claude sessions run by Ludovic) write most pull requests, review them, merge them and answer reports. Everything an agent posts on GitHub says so ("Opened by Ludovic's AI agent"). Contributors send pull requests from their forks like on any open-source project. Players report bugs on Discord and GitHub. Kira, the Discord bot, files their reports as issues. Releases are automatic: every merged change that players run ships within the hour. What could go wrong before (October 2026) Instructions hidden in a report. Someone could write "ignore your previous instructions and…" in a Discord message or an issue. Agents read those reports while working with Ludovic's full GitHub account. A check that counted as passed without running. Adding a label to a pull request started a second run of the checks in which verify was skipped , and GitHub counts a skipped required check as passed. Two pull requests merged before their real check had finished. Every release went straight to every player. A broken or malicious build reached every launcher within minutes, with nobody looking at it first. Downloads trusted GitHub alone. Anyone who got hold of a token that can write to the repository could replace a release's files, and launchers and servers would install them. The release machinery was ordinary code. A pull request could change the workflows that build and publish releases as easily as it changes a texture. Where things stand (19 October 2026) The next section describes the design once every part is in place. Some parts are live, some are waiting to merge, and some are waiting for Ludovic: Part Today verify always runs Live (#1010). Fork pull requests need approval Live : every outside contributor's workflows wait for a maintainer's approval. Private vulnerability reporting Live (see the end of this page). Signed checksums on releases Live for new releases (#1011): the release environment holds the key, and its public half is in release-keys.txt (#1023). Releases from before then are unsigned. Launchers and servers checking signatures Not yet : #1014 waits as a draft until a signed stable game release and a signed launcher release exist. Until then they trust GitHub's checksum, as before. Smoke test and release-blocker before publishing Live : since 2026-10-23 every release is the latest at once (one channel, Ludovic's decision), so it is published only after its smoke test passed and while no release-blocker is open. The 6-hour beta of the old Alpha, then stable flow (#1012) is gone. Reports marked suspicious Partly : the scan of Discord for agents does it. Kira's issues do it once its pull request merges. x: A server's levels: one per dimension Vanilla's MinecraftServer holds a ServerLevel per dimension, and each player is in one of them. Rusty Minecraft's server does the same. That covers the dedicated server and single player's server thread ( Game::serving , the default since #1114). So a LAN world's host and each guest can be in different dimensions at the same time. How the single-level Game maps onto vanilla's levels The game's tick code reads one level: the one held in Game 's own fields (the world, its streaming and save, block ticks, entities, block entities and their per-level queues). game/levels.rs keeps the other dimensions' levels as Parked values and swaps one into place ( enter_level ). The swap is mem::swap of each per-level field, so the tick code runs unchanged, one level at a time. Vanilla Rusty Minecraft MinecraftServer.levels the level in place plus Levels::parked MinecraftServer.tickChildren , every level tick_server : each level with a player in it, in Overworld, Nether, End order. The first pass reads the network and runs the shared parts (clock, weather, functions, autosave). ServerLevel.players Hub::here : the guests whose dimension is the level in place ServerPlayer.teleport into another level server_travel.rs : a Respawn packet, then the teleport once the destination has loaded (portals and execute in … tp ). An End gateway teleports within the End. PlayerList.respawn guest_respawn : into the respawn point's level, the Overworld unless the player has an anchor or a spawnpoint elsewhere ( Guest::respawn_elsewhere ), resolved through its block once that level has loaded ServerLevel.noPlayersEmptyTime , chunk unloading close_idle_levels : a level other than the Overworld with nobody in it for 300 ticks is saved and closed CommandSourceStack.getLevel with_source puts the source's level in place for a command ( execute in , execute at a player in another level) the levels' shared LevelData not swapped: game time, day time, weather, game rules, scoreboard, maps, entity ids ( next_entity , unique across levels) The packets of a guest are read in its own level's pass ( Hub::tick_level ), so its actions and commands run with its level in place. The window's own game ( --in-frame , --no-server-thread , HORIZON_SERVER_THREAD=0 , and the command harness) keeps one level, which follows its player ( enter_dimension ). LAN guests of a world run that way stay in the host's dimension. That mode is deprecated: never use it, it will be removed soon. It gets no multi-level work and no compatibility.
